newsitem.title: PERU: Peru's Fujimori heads to Bolivia for crisis talks.
newsitem.headline: Peru's Fujimori heads to Bolivia for crisis talks.

text.p: Peru's President Alberto Fujimori was due to head on Saturday for Bolivia to meet President Gonzalo Sanchez Lozada whose ambassador in Lima -- one of 72 hostages held by Marxist rebels -- is reportedly showing signs of emotional breakdown.

Fujimori, who has been to Bolivia once before during the 88-day hostage crisis, will fly to the neighbouring Andean country at about 5 p.m. (2200 GMT) for a three-day visit, Government Palace officials in Lima said.
Earlier this week, Bolivia's ambassador Jorge Gumucio quarreled with a Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebel inside the besieged Japanese ambassador's residence, a police source said.
In the most serious episode of its kind known to have happened during the siege, the MRTA rebel threatened Gumucio with a gun before other hostages intervened to calm the ambassador, the source said.
Peruvian media said Gumucio suffered an attack of hysteria but La Paz officials said the ambassador reacted calmly when provoked by the rebel's "offensive" statements about Bolivia.
There have been frequent appeals on health grounds for the release of Gumucio, who is diabetic and has a history of heart and blood pressure problems.
But the rebels have held on to the only hostage from a country other than Peru and Japan in the hope of exchanging him for MRTA members jailed in Bolivia.

The rebels' main demand is the release of about 400 jailed comrades. Fujimori has publicly refused to consider this demand, but speculation has increased recently that the government is privateley considering making some minor releases.

Following Wednesday's round of face-to-face negotiations aimed at ending the siege peacefully, both sides are in a period of "reflection ... to analyse alternatives that make a solution viable", according to the talks' guarantors.

The guarantors -- Archbishop Juan Luis Cipriani for the Vatican, Canadian Ambassador Anthony Vincent and the top local Red Cross official Michel Minnig -- have given no sign that negotiations are progressing substantially. No date is set for the next negotiating round.
The three-man comission has spent the last few days scrambling between separate meetings with the government and rebels in a bid to find ways of advancing the negotiations.

Rebels occupying the residence released most hostages in the first weeks of the siege. But they have held onto those they consider the best bargaining chips, including Fujimori's brother Pedro, two cabinet ministers, the Japanese ambassador and a long list of Japanese businessmen.
